notes.note: The Gītā names laziness (ālasya) among the bonds of tamas (BhG 14.8) and among the marks of the tāmasa doer (BhG 18.28).
Laziness is a bond of tamas (BhG 14.8) and a Yoga obstacle defined by heaviness (YB 1.30).
Stiffness and torpor (Vism XIV) are lack of drive and unwieldiness; Vyāsa's sloth is not starting because of heaviness.
Stiffness and torpor (Vism XIV) are lack of drive and unwieldiness; Vyāsa's sloth is not starting because of heaviness.
Same word, different sense: for Vyāsa, greed for contact with objects; in TS, non-abstention from harming, falsehood, theft, unchastity and possessiveness.
Same word, different sense: non-abstention from the five in TS; the mind's greed for objects in the Yoga (YB 1.30).
Vyāsa glosses the obstacle 'wrong seeing' as erroneous cognition (viparyaya-jñāna): the same cognition, as a modification (YS 1.8) and as an obstacle to samādhi (YS 1.30).
Vyāsa glosses wrong seeing as erroneous cognition (viparyaya-jñāna): the same cognition, as an obstacle (YS 1.30) and as a modification (YS 1.8).
The Gītā says tamas binds by heedlessness, laziness and sleep (BhG 14.8); Vyāsa defines heedlessness as not cultivating the means of samādhi.
Heedlessness is a bond of tamas (BhG 14.8); Vyāsa defines it as not cultivating the means of samādhi.
In TS, heedless (pramatta) activity is what makes taking life into harming (TS 7.13) and heedlessness is a cause of bondage (TS 8.1); YB's pramāda is about neglecting the means of samādhi.
Vyāsa's pramāda is not cultivating the means of samādhi (YB 1.30); the Jain pramāda is the carelessness that makes harm (TS 7.13).
The Dhammapada calls heedlessness the path to death (Dhp 21); Vyāsa defines it as not cultivating the means of samādhi.
Vyāsa defines heedlessness as not cultivating the means of samādhi (YB 1.30); the Dhammapada makes it the path to death.

The Vism defines doubt (vicikicchā) by wavering and indecision, an obstacle to practice (Vism XIV), and in the suttas it concerns wholesome states (DN 2); Vyāsa's saṃśaya is any knowledge touching both sides.
Vyāsa's saṃśaya is knowledge touching both sides (YB 1.30); the Vism's doubt is wavering that obstructs practice.

Vyāsa defines styāna as unfitness for work (akarmaṇyatā); the Vism defines torpor (middha) as unwieldiness (akammaññatā) and stiffness (thīna, the Pali form of the word styāna) as lack of drive. The words and the definitions cross over.
Vyāsa's styāna is the mind's unfitness for work (YB 1.30); Vism XIV's torpor is unwieldiness and its stiffness (thīna) lack of drive.
Vism III: the intelligent temperament is akin to the hating: as hate shuns beings, understanding shuns formations; alike in behaviour, opposite in quality.
Akin in behaviour, opposite in moral quality (Vism III).
The hating temperament is one in whom hate predominates (Vism III).
The temperament is a predominance of hate; hate itself is defined in Vism XIV.
Vism III: the speculative temperament is akin to the deluded: as delusion is restless through not penetrating, thought is restless through quick imagining.
Akin in behaviour (Vism III).

The Gītā's tamas is a strand of nature marked by delusion, heedlessness, laziness and sleep (BhG 14.8, 14.13); the Vism's deluded temperament is a predominance of delusion in a person, with stiffness, torpor and doubt among its frequent states (Vism III). Different frameworks.
Different frameworks: a strand of nature (BhG 14.8, 14.13), a predominance in a person (Vism III); both marked by delusion and dullness.
The deluded temperament is one in whom delusion predominates (Vism III).
The temperament is a predominance of delusion; delusion itself is defined in Vism XIV.
Vism III: the faithful temperament is akin (sabhāga) to the greedy: as greed seeks sense objects, faith seeks virtue; in behaviour alike, in moral quality opposite.
Akin in behaviour, opposite in moral quality (Vism III).

The Gītā's rajas is a strand of nature in all beings, marked by greed and passion (BhG 14.7, 14.12); the Vism's greedy temperament is a predominance of greed in a person's make-up, marked by posture, work, eating and seeing (Vism III). Different frameworks; both marked by greed.
Different frameworks: a strand of nature in the Gītā (BhG 14.7, 14.12), a predominance in a person in the Vism; both marked by greed.
The Vism lists deceit (māyā) and fraud among the states frequent in the greedy temperament (Vism III).
The Vism lists deceit (māyā) and fraud among the states frequent in the greedy temperament (Vism III).
The greedy temperament is one in whom greed predominates (Vism III).
The temperament is a predominance of greed; greed itself is defined in Vism XIV.
MN 10 names the scattered mind (vikkhitta citta) to be known as such, without describing it; Vyāsa's distracted ground is where samādhi is subordinate to distraction.
Vyāsa's distracted ground (vikṣipta) is where samādhi is subordinate to distraction (YB 1.1); MN 10 names the scattered mind without description.
MN 10 names the scattered mind without describing it; Vism XIV calls restlessness 'distraction of mind' (citta-vikkhepa).
MN 10 names the scattered mind without describing it; Vism XIV calls restlessness 'distraction of mind' (citta-vikkhepa).
Gauḍapāda's distraction (vikṣepa) is the mind scattered among desires and enjoyments, to be calmed (GK 3.42, 3.44); Vyāsa's distracted ground is a level of the mind in the Yoga's scheme.
Gauḍapāda's distraction (vikṣepa) is the mind scattered among desires and enjoyments, to be calmed (GK 3.42, 3.44); Vyāsa's distracted ground is a level of the mind in the Yoga's scheme.
Vyāsa's dejection is the mind's agitation when a wish is thwarted (YB 1.31); Arjuna's viṣāda is a collapse before a duty, confused about dharma (BhG 2.7).
Vyāsa's dejection is the mind's agitation when a wish is thwarted (YB 1.31); Arjuna's viṣāda is a collapse before a duty, confused about dharma (BhG 2.7).
Vyāsa's dejection is the mind's agitation when a wish is thwarted (YB 1.31); TS's sorrowful dwelling fixes the mind on removing the unpleasant or regaining the pleasant.
Vyāsa's dejection is the mind's agitation when a wish is thwarted (YB 1.31); TS's sorrowful dwelling fixes the mind on removing the unpleasant or regaining the pleasant.

Both name not-seeing as the root of bondage. YS avidyā is the fourfold mis-taking of YS 2.5 and ends in the seer's aloneness; the Theravāda avijjā/moha is blindness of mind and the root of all unwholesome states (Vism XIV), with no self to be uncovered. Theravāda denies the self the Yoga affirms.
Both name not-seeing as the root of bondage; the Yoga's avidyā ends in the seer's aloneness (YS 2.25), the Theravāda avijjā is cut by the fourth path with no self uncovered.
The fetter list names avijjā; Vism XIV defines moha. The Abhidhamma treats these as one factor, but that equation is not cited here.
The fetter list names avijjā; Vism XIV defines moha. The Abhidhamma treats these as one factor, but that equation is not cited here.
The same kind of lust named in two lists: as a hindrance it blocks jhāna (Vism IV); as a fetter it binds to the sense sphere and is abandoned only by the third path (Vism XXII).
The same kind of lust in two lists: hindrance to jhāna (Vism IV), fetter to the sense sphere (Vism XXII).
Vism XIV defines greed; sensual lust is its sense-sphere form as a fetter.
Vism XIV defines greed; sensual lust is its sense-sphere form as a fetter.
Theravāda conceit is haughtiness and self-exaltation (Vism XIV).
The Gītā lists arrogance and conceit (darpa, abhimāna) among demonic qualities (BhG 16.4).
Jain pride is one of four passions graded by intensity (TS 8.9); Theravāda conceit is haughtiness remaining until the fourth path (Vism XIV, XXII).
Theravāda conceit is haughtiness and self-exaltation, remaining until the fourth path (Vism XIV, XXII); Jain pride is a passion graded in four intensities.
Conceit (māna) is haughtiness and self-exaltation (Vism XIV); asmitā is the seeming oneness of seer and seeing. Related in the 'I am' they share, different in definition.
Asmitā is the seeming oneness of seer and seeing (YS 2.6); conceit is haughtiness and self-exaltation (Vism XIV).
Resentment (paṭigha) as a fetter binds to the sense sphere until the third path (Vism XXII); Vyāsa uses pratigha in defining dveṣa.
Vyāsa uses the word pratigha in defining dveṣa (YB 2.8).
Ill will as a hindrance blocks jhāna; resentment (paṭigha) as a fetter binds to the sense sphere until the third path (Vism XXII).
Ill will in the hindrance list, resentment in the fetter list (Vism IV, XXII).
Vism XIV defines hate; resentment is its form as a fetter.
Vism XIV defines hate; resentment is its form as a fetter.

Both name a false taking of something as self. YS 2.6 confuses the instrument (buddhi) with a real seer that the Yoga affirms; personality view regards any of the five aggregates as self (Vism XVII), and Theravāda affirms no self at all. That denial stands.
Both name a false taking of something as self; the Yoga affirms a real seer beyond buddhi (YS 2.6), Theravāda denies any self (Vism XVII). The denial stands.
In the hindrance restlessness is paired with remorse and blocks jhāna; as a fetter, restlessness alone remains until the fourth path (Vism XXII).
Paired with remorse as a hindrance to jhāna; alone as a higher fetter until the fourth path.
The same mental factor (Vism XIV) named in two lists: as a hindrance it blocks jhāna (Vism IV); as a fetter it binds to rebirth and is cut by the first path (Vism XXII).
The same mental factor named in the list of hindrances and the list of fetters; the roles differ (blocks jhāna / binds to rebirth).
The same desire and anger of the Gītā, here shown as links in a chain (BhG 2.62–63) and there named as the one enemy (3.37).
The same desire and anger of the Gītā, here shown as links in a chain (BhG 2.62–63) and there named as the one enemy (3.37).
YS rāga follows remembered pleasure (YS 2.7); the Gītā's attachment and desire grow from dwelling on objects (BhG 2.62).
YS rāga follows remembered pleasure (YS 2.7); the Gītā's attachment and desire grow from dwelling on objects (BhG 2.62).
Jain pride (māna) is one of four passions (TS 8.9); the Gītā lists arrogance and conceit (darpa, abhimāna) among demonic qualities.
The Gītā lists arrogance and conceit among demonic qualities (BhG 16.4).
Jain deceit (māyā) and the Gītā's hypocrisy (dambha) overlap in showing what one is not.
The Gītā lists hypocrisy (dambha) among demonic qualities (BhG 16.4).
Desire and anger are born of rajas (BhG 3.37).
Born of rajas (BhG 3.37).
Jain anger is a passion that makes the soul take in karmic matter (TS 8.2, 8.9); the Gītā's anger is born of rajas and covers knowledge.
The Gītā's anger is born of desire and of rajas (BhG 2.62, 3.37).
Vyāsa counts anger within dveṣa, following remembered pain (YB 2.8); the Gītā derives anger from desire (BhG 2.62).
Vyāsa counts anger within dveṣa, following remembered pain (YB 2.8); the Gītā derives anger from desire (BhG 2.62).
The Gītā's desire (kāma) is born of rajas and grows from attachment to objects dwelt on (BhG 2.62, 3.37); YS rāga follows remembered pleasure. Both place desire before anger.
The Gītā's desire (kāma) is born of rajas and grows from attachment to objects dwelt on (BhG 2.62, 3.37); YS rāga follows remembered pleasure. Both place desire before anger.
Theravāda dosa is ferocity, a root of the unwholesome (Vism XIV); the Gītā's anger is born of desire and of rajas.
Theravāda dosa is ferocity, a root of the unwholesome (Vism XIV); the Gītā's anger is born of desire and of rajas.
Gauḍapāda's distraction is the mind scattered among desires and enjoyments, to be calmed (GK 3.42, 3.44).
Gauḍapāda's distraction is the mind scattered among desires and enjoyments, to be calmed (GK 3.42, 3.44).
The Kaṭha's senses run like vicious horses when the mind is unyoked (KU 1.3.5); the Gītā's turbulent senses carry off the mind (BhG 2.60).
The Gītā's turbulent senses carry off the mind (BhG 2.60, 2.67); the Kaṭha's senses run like vicious horses when the mind is unyoked (KU 1.3.5).
Theravāda restlessness is disquiet, like water whipped by wind (Vism XIV); the Gītā's mind is as hard to hold as the wind (BhG 6.34). Similar image, different frameworks.
The Gītā's restless mind is as hard to hold as the wind (BhG 6.34); Vism XIV's restlessness is like water whipped by wind.
Gauḍapāda's no-mind state is brahman when the mind neither dissolves nor scatters (GK 3.46); the fourth is described by negation (MāU 7). Both in the Advaita reading of the Māṇḍūkya.
Gauḍapāda's no-mind state is brahman when the mind neither dissolves nor scatters (GK 3.46); the fourth is described by negation (MāU 7). Both in the Advaita reading of the Māṇḍūkya.
YS describes kleśas that remain dormant or thinned (YS 2.4); GK 3.44 asks that the still-coloured mind be recognised. Related idea of a latent residue, in different systems.
YS describes kleśas that remain dormant or thinned (YS 2.4); GK 3.44 asks that the still-coloured mind be recognised. Related idea of a latent residue, in different systems.
Gauḍapāda's laya is the mind dissolving as in sleep during stilling (GK 3.35, 3.44); tamas binds by sleep (BhG 14.8).
Gauḍapāda's laya is the mind dissolving as in sleep during stilling (GK 3.35, 3.44); tamas binds by sleep (BhG 14.8).
Torpor in the Vism can show as nodding and sleep (Vism XIV); GK's laya is the mind dissolving as in sleep. Both are to be roused; the frameworks differ.
Gauḍapāda's laya is the mind dissolving as in sleep (GK 3.35, 3.44); torpor can show as nodding and sleep (Vism XIV).
Gauḍapāda's laya is the mind dissolving as it does in deep sleep (GK 3.35, 3.44).
Gauḍapāda's laya is the mind dissolving as it does in deep sleep (GK 3.35, 3.44).
Gauḍapāda warns against savouring the happiness of stillness (GK 3.45); YS warns against taking powers as accomplishments. Both are attachments to fruits along the way.
Gauḍapāda warns against savouring the happiness of stillness (GK 3.45); YS warns against taking powers as accomplishments. Both are attachments to fruits along the way.
The Vism's attachment (nikanti) to light, rapture and bliss is the one imperfection that is also unwholesome (Vism XX); GK 3.45 warns against savouring the happiness of stillness.
Gauḍapāda: do not savour the happiness of stillness (GK 3.45); Vism: attachment to these states is the imperfection that is also unwholesome (Vism XX).
Restlessness in the Vism is disquiet, 'distraction of mind' (Vism XIV); GK's vikṣepa is scattering among desires. Different frameworks.
Restlessness in the Vism is disquiet, 'distraction of mind' (Vism XIV); GK's vikṣepa is scattering among desires. Different frameworks.
The guṇas are not separate things in a person but three strands that overpower one another in turn (BhG 14.10).
The guṇas are not separate things in a person but three strands that overpower one another in turn (BhG 14.10).
The Gītā says rajas springs from craving and attachment (BhG 14.7).
The Gītā says rajas springs from craving and attachment (BhG 14.7).
The Gītā's tamas is born of ignorance and deludes (BhG 14.8); Vism's moha is blindness of mind.
The Gītā's tamas is born of ignorance and deludes (BhG 14.8); Vism's moha is blindness of mind.
Both stand first among the roots of bondage in their systems (YS 2.3–4; TS 8.1). Jain wrong view is the absence of faith in the reals as the Jain teaching sets them out (TS 1.2); the reals differ.
Both stand first among the roots of bondage in their systems (TS 8.1; YS 2.4); the reals they concern differ.
In TS heedlessness is a cause of bondage (TS 8.1).
The Dhammapada's heedlessness is the path to death (Dhp 21).

The Jain 'cruel meditation' is dwelling that arises from harming, falsehood, theft and guarding one's possessions (TS 9.35); YS vitarkas are thoughts of violating the restraints, met by cultivating the opposite.
YS 2.34's vitarkas are thoughts of harming and the rest, met by cultivating the opposite; TS 9.35's cruel dwelling arises from harming, falsehood, theft and guarding possessions.
Vyāsa lists krodha within dveṣa; the Jain krodha is one of the four passions with four intensities (TS 8.9). Same word, different system.
Vyāsa lists anger within dveṣa (YB 2.8); the Jain krodha is a passion graded in four intensities that binds karmic matter (TS 8.2, 8.9).
Jain anger is a passion graded in four intensities (TS 8.9).
Theravāda hate is a momentary mental factor, a root of the unwholesome (Vism XIV); Jain anger is a passion by which the soul takes in karmic matter.
Jain greed is one of four passions that make the soul take in karmic matter (TS 8.2, 8.9); YS rāga is a kleśa rooted in avidyā. Similar pull, different account of bondage.
Vyāsa glosses rāga with the word lobha (YB 2.7).
Jain greed is a passion that makes the soul take in karmic matter (TS 8.2, 8.9).
Theravāda greed is a mental factor that grasps like monkey-lime (Vism XIV); Jain greed is a passion that binds karmic matter (TS 8.2).
Asmitā is the seeming oneness of seer and seeing (YS 2.6), not pride as such; related only through the 'I'.
Asmitā is the seeming oneness of seer and seeing (YS 2.6), not pride as such; related only through the 'I'.
The Kaṭha sets the pleasant within ignorance (avidyā) and the good with knowledge (KU 1.2.4–5); YS avidyā is the mis-taking of YS 2.5.
The Kaṭha sets the pleasant within ignorance (avidyā) and the good with knowledge (KU 1.2.4–5); YS avidyā is the mis-taking of YS 2.5.
The Kaṭha calls the body the chariot of the self (KU 1.3.3); the Taittirīya calls it the self made of food (TU 2.1.1).
The Kaṭha calls the body the chariot of the self (KU 1.3.3); the Taittirīya calls it the self made of food (TU 2.1.1).
In the Kaṭha the mind is the reins (KU 1.3.3); in the Taittirīya the self made of mind is the third 'self'.
In the Kaṭha the mind is the reins (KU 1.3.3); in the Taittirīya the self made of mind is the third 'self'.
In the Kaṭha understanding (buddhi) is the charioteer (KU 1.3.3); in the Taittirīya the self made of understanding is the fourth 'self'.
In the Kaṭha understanding (buddhi) is the charioteer (KU 1.3.3); in the Taittirīya the self made of understanding is the fourth 'self'.

Vyāsa's 'may I be' is close to the craving for being (bhava-taṇhā) named in DN 22; YS treats it as a kleśa grounded in avidyā about a real self, DN 22 as craving that makes for renewed being, with no self.
Vyāsa's 'may I be' (YB 2.9) is close to the craving for being (DN 22).
Vism XIV defines moha as blindness of mind that hides the nature of the object; YS avidyā as mis-taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self. Similar function, different metaphysics.
Both are the root not-seeing of their systems; the metaphysics differ (YS 2.5; Vism XIV).
Vyāsa (on YS 1.8) calls erroneous cognition 'avidyā of five parts': the same error seen as a modification of mind (vṛtti) and as an affliction (kleśa).
Vyāsa calls erroneous cognition avidyā of five parts: the same error, as a modification of mind (vṛtti) and as an affliction (kleśa).
Ill will as a hindrance is named for blocking the mind's continuous flow on its object (Vism IV); YS dveṣa is a kleśa following remembered pain.
Ill will as a hindrance is named for blocking the mind's continuous flow on its object (Vism IV); YS dveṣa is a kleśa following remembered pain.
Theravāda dosa is ferocity, like a struck snake (Vism XIV); Vyāsa's dveṣa includes resentment, the wish to strike and anger toward remembered pain. Similar, in different maps.
Vyāsa's dveṣa includes resentment, the wish to strike and anger toward remembered pain (YB 2.8).
Sensual desire as a hindrance is named for what it blocks: the mind's settling on one object (Vism IV). YS rāga covers any remembered pleasure and its means.
YS rāga follows remembered pleasure (YS 2.7); the hindrance is sensual desire that blocks concentration (Vism IV).

Vyāsa himself glosses rāga with the word lobha (YB 2.7). The Theravāda lobha is a mental factor that grasps its object like bird-lime (Vism XIV), one of three roots, with no self behind it; YS rāga is a kleśa growing in the field of avidyā.
Vyāsa glosses rāga with the word lobha (YB 2.7); the Theravāda lobha is a momentary mental factor with no self behind it (Vism XIV).
Craving (taṇhā) arises where there is what is dear and agreeable (DN 22); Vyāsa uses the word tṛṣṇā in defining rāga. Different frameworks (kleśa vs origin of suffering).
Vyāsa defines rāga with the word tṛṣṇā (YB 2.7); craving in DN 22 is the origin of suffering, with no self.
Muddled mindfulness (MN 118) and heedlessness (Dhp 21) are named in different texts; both are the opposite of the attending the suttas ask for.
Muddled mindfulness (MN 118) and heedlessness (Dhp 21) are named in different texts; both are the opposite of the attending the suttas ask for.
Vism XIV defines hate; the hindrance is ill will as it blocks the mind's flow.
Vism XIV defines hate; the hindrance is ill will as it blocks the mind's flow.
Vism XIV defines greed; sensual desire as a hindrance is named for what it blocks.
Vism XIV defines greed; sensual desire as a hindrance is named for what it blocks.
The Vism says torpor (middha) can show as nodding and sleep; YS sleep is itself a modification of mind. Related, not the same.
The Vism says torpor (middha) can show as nodding and sleep; YS sleep is itself a modification of mind. Related, not the same.
The Māṇḍūkya calls the deep-sleep self (prājña) 'made of bliss, enjoyer of bliss' (MāU 5); the Taittirīya's self made of bliss is the innermost of the five, with brahman as its support.
Prājña is 'made of bliss' (MāU 5), as the innermost self of the Taittirīya is (TU 2.5.1).
Apāna is the left side of the self made of breath (TU 2.2.1).
Apāna is the left side of the self made of breath (TU 2.2.1).
In TU 2.2.1 prāṇa is the head of the self made of breath; Vyāsa locates prāṇa in mouth and nose up to the heart (YB 3.39).
Prāṇa is the head of the self made of breath (TU 2.2.1).
Vyāna is the right side of the self made of breath (TU 2.2.1).
Vyāna is the right side of the self made of breath (TU 2.2.1).

The Vism's imperfections of insight (light, rapture, bliss and the rest) become imperfections when taken for the path (Vism XX); YS 3.37 calls powers obstacles in samādhi. Similar warning, different paths.
YS 3.37 calls powers obstacles in samādhi; the Vism calls lights and bliss imperfections when taken for the path.

YS counts sleep as a modification whose content is absence; the Māṇḍūkya calls deep sleep the third quarter, a mass of knowing, made of bliss (MāU 5), and Gauḍapāda calls it not knowing the real (GK 1.15). Same state, different accounts.
YS counts sleep as a modification of mind to be stilled (YS 1.10); the Māṇḍūkya makes deep sleep a quarter of the self (MāU 5).
Vyāsa says memory in dream has an imagined object; the Māṇḍūkya's dream state is inward-knowing, enjoying the subtle (MāU 4).
Vyāsa says memory in dream has an imagined object; the Māṇḍūkya's dream state is inward-knowing, enjoying the subtle (MāU 4).
